h1: Target hops for robust bittering in English ales
title: Target Hops for Bittering English Ales | Craft Beer School
desc: How to use Target hops for bittering English ales: alpha range, a worked IBU sum for 1,000 litres and where its strong flavour helps or hurts.
teaser: Target bitters an English ale with half the hop mass of Fuggle. Put it late in the boil and it bites back.
standfirst: Target is the English high alpha workhorse. It is cheap bitterness per IBU with a pungent, herbal edge. Here is how to dose it, where to keep it and when to choose something gentler.
sections: Target is a bittering hop with opinions

Target came out of the Wye College breeding programme in Kent in the early 1970s. It was bred for wilt resistance and high alpha acid at a time when English growers were losing gardens to verticillium wilt. Alpha acid usually runs from about 9 to 12.5%, roughly double a Fuggle or a Golding.

That makes it an efficient kettle hop. The catch is flavour. Target is not neutral like Magnum. Brewers describe it as pungent, herbal and sage-like, with some citrus and a firm, slightly coarse bitterness when it is overdone. In a 4% bitter that edge can be a feature. In a delicate golden ale it can take over.
The sum: half the hop mass for the same bitterness

Take a 1,000 litre best bitter aimed at 35 IBU, with one 60 minute addition and about 28% utilisation in a commercial kettle. The working is grams = IBU x litres / (alpha x utilisation x 1,000).

  • Target at 11% alpha: 35 x 1,000 / (0.11 x 0.28 x 1,000) = about 1,140 g.
  • Fuggle at 5% alpha: 35 x 1,000 / (0.05 x 0.28 x 1,000) = 2,500 g.

Less than half the pellets means less vegetable matter in the kettle, a smaller trub cone in the whirlpool and less wort lost with it. On a 10 hl brewhouse that loss is small per brew. Over a year of weekly brews it shows up in your yield figures.

The floor detail we care about here is the certificate of analysis that comes with each lot. Target from one harvest might test at 9.8% and the next at 12.1%. Brew the second lot on the first lot's weights and your bitter gains around 8 IBU. Regulars notice that. Put the lot number and its alpha on the brew sheet and redo the sum each time a new box is opened.

Storage matters as much as the label. Alpha acids degrade with heat and oxygen. A carton that spent a week in a warm warehouse in Chennai is not the carton the lab tested. Keep pellets vacuum or nitrogen packed in a freezer below 0 °C. Our guide on sourcing malt and hops in India covers the cold chain from port to brewery.
Where Target belongs in the boil

Most brewers use Target for the first addition only, at 60 to 90 minutes. They finish with a softer English variety. A common pattern for a best bitter is 70 to 80% of the IBUs from Target, with the rest from late Goldings or Fuggle for aroma.

Late additions of Target are possible but need care. At 10 or 15 minutes it adds a strong herbal, slightly catty note that some drinkers love in a porter and others find harsh in a pale ale. If you want to try it, use it at no more than 0.5 g per litre late and taste the result against a control.

Target earns its place where malt is strong enough to carry it:

  • Best and strong bitters, especially with crystal malt at 5 to 10% of the grist.
  • Porters and stouts, where roast flavours absorb the herbal edge.
  • English IPAs at 40 to 60 IBU, bittered with Target and finished with Goldings.
  • Old ales and barley wines, where a long boil and high gravity need a lot of bitterness.

It is a weaker choice for pale lagers or anything where a clean, quiet bitterness is the goal. Our guide on First Gold covers a softer English option.

Most Indian brewpubs pour lagers, wheat beers and pale ales, so an English bitter is often a seasonal or a tap for the regulars who ask for one. That is a good reason to keep a high alpha English hop on the shelf. A 5 kg carton of Target goes a long way when each 1,000 litre batch needs a little over a kilo.

Serve temperature changes how its bitterness reads. Poured at 3 °C from a lager line, an English bitter tastes thin and the Target edge sticks out. Poured nearer 10 to 12 °C, the malt comes forward and the bitterness sits behind it. If you have one tap you can run a little warmer, give it to the bitter.

If Target is out of stock, Admiral or Challenger can stand in for bittering. Scale by alpha, not by weight. Northdown works too. Going the other way, Target can replace Northern Brewer in many English recipes as long as late additions are cut back.

What no substitution table tells you is how the bitterness feels. Two beers at 35 IBU can taste very different depending on cohumulone, oil content and the malt behind them. Measuring and reasoning about that is where a brewer moves past recipe copying.
faqs: What is the alpha acid content of Target hops?
Target usually tests at about 9 to 12.5% alpha acid. Always use the figure on the lot's certificate of analysis rather than a typical range.
Can Target be used as an aroma hop?
It can, but it is strong. Late additions give a pungent, herbal note that suits porters better than pale ales. Most brewers keep it in the bittering slot.
Admiral, Challenger or Northdown are the usual English swaps for bittering. Recalculate the weight from the new hop's alpha acid.
